sourceIssues.printed: w ∈ N_G(M)/M
sourceIssues.correction: Replace N_G(M)/M by the absolute Weyl group W(G, T) of a maximal torus T ⊂ M with μ ∈ X_*(T), as in Proposition 1.1.13. Equivalently: some G(Q̄_p)-conjugate μ′ of μ factoring through T makes ([b_M], {μ′}) M-admissible.
sourceIssues.reason: The printed statement fails already for split G. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1 × GL_2 (blocks of sizes 1 and 2), μ = (0,1,0) and b_M = diag(p,1,1), which is basic in M. Then ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible: its Newton point (1,0,0) equals the dominant μ̄, and both have κ_G = 1. But κ_M(b_M) = (1,0), while κ_M(μ) = (0,1). Since the blocks have different sizes, N_G(M) = M, so W(G, M) is trivial and no w in it helps. The permutation of the first two coordinates, in W(G, T) = S_3, does. The proof transports to the quasi-split inner form and applies Proposition 1.1.13. That proposition gives w* in the absolute Weyl group W(G*, T*), not in N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so the proof establishes the corrected statement. The only use is in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17, p.13, for G not necessarily quasi-split. It cites "Lemma 1.1.13" (the quasi-split Proposition 1.1.13) in the form w ∈ W(G, T). The corrected Corollary 1.1.15 is exactly what that step needs, so the later results stand. Checked on the page images. Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 2, items N29 and N32), which also verified the Weyl-group computation by machine.

review.reason: Checked on the page images of pp.11–12. The counterexample holds. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1×GL_2, μ = (0,1,0) (G-minuscule, factoring through M) and b_M = diag(p,1,1). Then b_M is basic in M, with Newton point (1,0,0) central in M. The pair is G-admissible: ν = (1,0,0) = μ̄, and κ_G = 1 = |μ|. But κ_M(b_M) = (1,0) and κ_M(μ) = (0,1). N_G(M) preserves the eigenspaces of Z_M = {diag(a,b,b)}, of dimensions 1 and 2, so N_G(M) = M. Therefore no w ∈ N_G(M)/M works, while the transposition (12) ∈ W(G,T) does. The proof fails at exactly one step: Proposition 1.1.13 produces an element of W(G*,T*), not of N_{G*}(M*)/M*. Everything else in the proof is compatible with the corrected statement. Corollary 1.1.15 is never cited by number. Its intended use is the step 'By Lemma 1.1.13, there exists w ∈ W(G,T)' in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17 (p.13), where G may be non-quasi-split, and that step needs exactly the corrected form. So Corollary 1.1.17, Proposition 1.2.5 and the main theorems stand. VERIFY.md records no known erratum. Defence considered: W(G,M) is explicitly defined as N_G(M)/M and the proof explicitly identifies it with N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so this is not a notational slip.

review.reason: Checked on the page image (p.20) and in two independent readings. The D^× computation was redone: b ↦ bΠ identifies B(D^×) with B(GL_2), raising κ by 1 and the Newton slopes by 1/2, and a slope of multiplicity 1 in a 2-dimensional isocrystal is an integer. The global instance (a quaternionic Shimura curve ramified at p) is of Hodge type. For quasi-split G_{Q_p} everything holds: [b_μ] is the image of κ_{T*}^{-1}([μ^{-1}]). The same place also has: Quotation checked on the p.3 image. Theorem 3 is the introduction's form of Corollary 1.3.16 (p.20), which uses the μ-ordinary stratum S_[b_μ] of §1.3.15. §1.3.15 asserts for arbitrary G_{Q_p}, without proof, that 'There is a unique [b_μ] ∈ B(G_{Q_p},{μ^{-1}}) with N_ξ(ν̄_G([b_μ])) = μ̄^{-1}'. Uniqueness is fine by (1.1.2.3). Existence fails for non-quasi-split G. Independent check: take B an indefinite quaternion algebra over Q ramified at p, G = B^× (PEL, hence Hodge type), G_{Q_p} = D^×, G* = GL_2, μ = (1,0). Identify D^×(L) = GL_2(L) with Frobenius Ad(Π)∘σ, where Π = [[0,1],[p,0]] and Π² = p. Then b ↦ bΠ is a bijection B(D^×) → B(GL_2), because (bΠ)σ(bΠ)⋯ = (b·σ_D(b)⋯)·(Πσ(Π)⋯). It raises κ by 1, and it adds the central (1/2,1/2) to Newton points. A class with ν = (0,−1) would give a 2-dimensional isocrystal with the distinct slopes 1/2 and −1/2, each of multiplicity 1. That is impossible, since slope r/s in lowest terms occurs with multiplicity divisible by s. Hence [b_μ] does not exist. The only admissible class is basic, with ν = (−1/2,−1/2), and a check against (1.1.5.2) shows no non-basic class is admissible. So 'the μ-ordinary locus' in Theorem 3 is undefined for such data, and the proof, which goes through §1.3.15, covers only the case where [b_μ] exists. With G_{Q_p} quasi-split everything holds: [b_μ] is the image of κ_{T*}^{-1}([μ^{-1}]), and (1.1.3.1) holds by 1.1.3. Case for the defence: (i) p.2 presents Theorem 3 as a generalisation of Wedhorn and Wortmann, whose setting is hyperspecial, hence quasi-split. (ii) In the D^× test case the hypothesis of Theorem 3 fails at parahoric level: the Čerednik–Drinfeld model is semistable, with nodes where two components meet, so its special fibre is not locally integral. The test case therefore shows that the statement is ill-defined, not that a density assertion is false. No non-quasi-split example with a locally integral special fibre and no [b_μ] is exhibited, so 'false' should not be claimed; 'not established / not well-defined as stated' is accurate. (iii) Reading 'μ-ordinary' as 'the maximal element of B(G,{μ^{-1}})' would need (1.1.3.1) for that class, which the paper does not supply in the non-quasi-split case. On the claim's secondary point: whenever [b_μ] exists, (1.1.3.1) does hold, at least when G is an extended pure inner form of G* (as for D^×). Twisting by a basic x chosen in the Levi M* = Cent(μ̄*) puts a representative of [b_μ] in the Q_p-Levi J_x(M*) with central Q_p-rational Newton point. That point is a routine omission, not part of the mistake. Scope: this is the same defect as ledger E8 (§1.3.15, already 'error / a stated result'), not an independent mistake. review.reason: Not a mistake: the two formulas define the same group. Aut(A_s0), the automorphisms in the prime-to-p isogeny category, lies in End_Q(A_s0)^× = Aut_Q(A_s0)(Q). I_s0 is a closed Q-subgroup of Aut_Q(A_s0). A Q-point of Aut_Q(A_s0) that satisfies the Q-rational equations of I_s0 over Q_p lies in I_s0(Q). Hence I_s0(Q_p) ∩ Aut(A_s0) = I_s0(Q) ∩ Aut(A_s0), which is the expression on p.22. Writing Q would match the notation I(Z_(p)) better, but the printed formula is correct. Independent check: Checked on the image: p.21 has 'I_{s0}(Z_(p)) = I_{s0}(Q_p) ∩ Aut(A_{s0})' and p.22 (end of the proof of Lemma 2.1.4) has 'I_{s0}(Z_(p)) = I_{s0}(Q) ∩ Aut(A_{s0})'. These define the same group. Aut(A_{s0}) in the prime-to-p isogeny category lies in (End(A_{s0}) ⊗ Z_(p))^× ⊂ Aut_Q(A_{s0})(Q) ⊂ Aut_Q(A_{s0})(Q_p), so the p.21 intersection makes sense. I_{s0} is a closed Q-subgroup of Aut_Q(A_{s0}), cut out by polynomial equations with Q-coefficients. A Q-point that lies in I_{s0}(Q_p) satisfies those equations, so it lies in I_{s0}(Q). Hence I_{s0}(Q_p) ∩ Aut(A_{s0}) = I_{s0}(Q) ∩ Aut(A_{s0}). The p.21 formula is correct as printed, only less idiomatic, so it should not be recorded as a mistake. I agree with the first reading's rejection.

review.reason: Checked on the p.10 image. The order ⪯_G of 1.1.1 (p.5) asks that ν_2 − ν_1 be a nonnegative linear combination of positive coroots with rational coefficients. It has to be rational there, because Newton points are fractional. With that order, 'μ′ ⪯_G μ and μ minuscule' does not imply that μ′ is conjugate to μ. Example: G = PGL_2, μ = ϖ^∨ (t ↦ diag(t,1)) and μ′ = 0. Then μ − μ′ = α^∨/2, so 0 ⪯ ϖ^∨, but 0 is not conjugate to ϖ^∨. The missing input is that μ′ and μ have the same image in π_1(G), and it is available in context. G is unramified, so the Kottwitz map w_G : G(L) → π_1(G) kills G(W) and N(L). With g = nm we get g^{−1}b_Mσ(g) = (m^{−1}b_Mσ(m))·n″ with n″ ∈ N(L). This element lies in G(W)μ(p)G(W), and m^{−1}b_Mσ(m) lies in M(W)μ′(p)M(W) ⊂ G(W)μ′(p)G(W). Hence μ^♮ = μ′^♮. So μ − μ′_dom is in the coroot lattice, with nonnegative rational and hence integral coefficients on the simple coroots. A minuscule dominant μ is minimal among dominant coweights in its class modulo coroots, so μ′_dom = μ. In the paper's defence, the sentence explains an argument that is cited ([LR87, Lem. 5.2]; alternatives [Kot03], [Kis17]), and that argument gives the integral order. Only the paraphrase, which pins down the order 'in the notation of 1.1.1', is insufficient.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Proposition 1.1.13, reduction to adjoint G, p.10
sourceIssues.printed: The kernel of the first map is the image of X_*(Z_G)_{Γ_p} → π_1(M)_{Γ_p}.
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the sentence by: 'After ⊗Q, coinvariants are exact, and the kernel of π_1(M) → π_1(M̃) is X_*(Z_G). Hence the kernel of the first map becomes, after ⊗Q, the image of X_*(Z_G)_{Γ_p} ⊗ Q.' Then continue: if x lies in both kernels, then x ⊗ 1 comes from (X_*(Z_G) ⊗ Q)_{Γ_p} and dies in (π_1(G) ⊗ Q)_{Γ_p}. Now X_*(Z_G)_Q → π_1(G)_Q is injective, because Z_G^0 → G^ab is an isogeny, and Q-coinvariants are exact, so x ⊗ 1 = 0 and x is torsion. By [CKV15, 2.5.12(2)], x = 0.
sourceIssues.reason: Taking coinvariants is only right exact, so the printed claim fails in general. Counterexample: G = SU(4)/μ_2, quasi-split over Q_p and split by a quadratic E/Q_p. Γ_p acts on X_*(T) through the diagram involution θ of A_3, and M = T is standard (the centralizer of the maximal split torus). Here X_*(Z_G) = 0. X_*(T) = Q^∨ + Zϖ_2^∨ has basis α_1^∨, α_2^∨, ϖ_2^∨. Since θα_1^∨ = α_3^∨ = 2ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − 2α_2^∨, we get (θ−1)X_*(T) = Z·2(ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − α_2^∨). So x = ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − α_2^∨ has order 2 in π_1(T)_{Γ_p}. Its image in π_1(M̃)_{Γ_p} = (P^∨)_{Γ_p} is ϖ_3^∨ − ϖ_1^∨ = 0. Thus the kernel is nonzero, while the image of X_*(Z_G)_{Γ_p} is 0. The case M = G is even simpler: π_1(G) = Z/2 ⊂ π_1(G^ad) = Z/4, with θ = −1, gives the zero map Z/2 → Z/2 on coinvariants. The conclusion drawn ('so the intersection must be a torsion group') still holds by the argument in the correction. So this is a false intermediate statement that does not break the proof. (Here x maps to the generator of π_1(G)_{Γ_p}, so it is not in the second kernel, which is consistent.)

review.reason: Checked on the p.10 image, and I re-derived the counterexample. Take G = SU(4)/μ_2, quasi-split over Q_p and split by a quadratic E/Q_p, with M = T the centralizer of a maximal split torus; this is a standard Levi. Then M̃ = T^ad and Z_G ≅ μ_2, so X_*(Z_G) = 0. In fundamental-coweight coordinates P^∨ = Z^3, X_*(T) = {(a,b,c) : a + c even} ⊃ Q^∨, and Γ_p acts through θ, which swaps a and c. So (θ−1)X_*(T) = {(d,0,−d) : d even}. The vector x = (−1,0,1) = ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − α_2^∨ lies in X_*(T) and has order 2 in X_*(T)_Γ. But x = (θ−1)ϖ_1^∨ is 0 in (P^∨)_Γ. So the kernel of π_1(M)_Γ → π_1(M̃)_Γ is nonzero, while the image of X_*(Z_G)_Γ is 0. (x maps to the nonzero element of π_1(G)_Γ = Z/2, which is consistent with CKV15.) The case M = G fails too: Z/2 → Z/4 → Z/2, with θ = −1 on Z/4, is the zero map on coinvariants. The cause is that coinvariants are only right exact. The printed claim is not idle. The next sentence ('so the intersection must be a torsion group') is deduced from it, so the proof of Proposition 1.1.13 fails at this step as written. That makes 'affects: the proof' the right reach, by the same standard as E5 and E9 (a printed step fails, the result survives after a repair). The conclusion does survive, as the correction shows, so no stated result is affected.

review.reason: Checked on the p.11 image. Having ξ(P) = P* rational does not make ξ(M) rational. If ξ has ξ(P) = P* and u ∈ R_u(P*)(Q̄_p), then int(u)∘ξ is again an inner twisting with the same property, and it moves ξ(M) to uξ(M)u^{−1}. Concretely, take G = G* = GL_2, P = B upper triangular, M the diagonal torus, and ξ = int(u) with u = (1 a; 0 1) and a ∈ Q̄_p∖Q_p. Then ξ(P) = B, but σ(ξ(M)) = ξ(M) would need u^{−1}σ(u) ∈ N(T), that is σ(a) = a for all σ, which fails. The proof then needs M* to be a Q_p-Levi (B(M*)_b, κ_{M*}, and 'B* ⊂ P*, T* ⊂ M*'), and only a rational M* makes ξ|_M an inner twisting. The repair is one extra normalization. P* has a Q_p-rational Levi factor, and all Levi factors of P* are R_u(P*)(Q̄_p)-conjugate, so after composing ξ with int(u) for some u ∈ R_u(P*)(Q̄_p) we have ξ(M) rational. Then ξ^{−1}σ(ξ) = int(g_σ) with g_σ ∈ N_G(P) ∩ N_G(M) = M, so ξ|_M is an inner twisting. The step is routine, and the proof is otherwise sound.

sourceIssues.reason: KP18 Cor. 0.3 (Publ. IHÉS 128, p.124; checked in the KP18 text) gives normality of the special fibre only 'If K°_p is associated to a point x which is a special vertex in B(G, Q_p^ur)'. It is stated under the introduction's standing assumptions, which include 'p does not divide the order |π_1(G^der)|' (p.122). Neither condition appears in Cor. 1.3.18. A parahoric that is special over Q_p need not be special over Q_p^ur. For the Shimura curve of an indefinite quaternion algebra B/Q ramified at an odd prime p, G_Qp = D^× splits over Q_{p^2} (tame), and K_p = O_D^× is the unique parahoric (the building is a point, so it is special). Over Q_p^ur, however, K_p becomes an Iwahori subgroup of GL_2. There [b_μ] does not exist (E8), and the Čerednik–Drinfeld special fibre has ordinary double points, so it is not locally integral. So the corollary fails in this case when 'special' has its usual meaning over Q_p. Defence: the authors may intend 'special' in KP18's sense (special over Q_p^ur). On that reading only the π_1 hypothesis is missing, and that hypothesis is not automatic for Hodge type (e.g. G^der ≅ SU(1,5)/μ_3 acting through Λ^3, where π_1 = Z/3).

review.reason: The p.20 image shows the quoted statement and proof. KP18 Cor. 0.3 (p.124 of the KP18 text) gives normality of the special fibre only 'If K°_p is associated to a point x which is a special vertex in B(G, Q_p^ur)'. It sits under the Introduction's standing assumptions (p.122): p > 2, abelian type, tame, and p ∤ |π_1(G^der)|. KMS assume only 'K_p is a special parahoric', which in the usual sense (Tits) means special in B(G, Q_p). By KP18's footnote, special over Q_p^ur (very special) points exist only for quasi-split G_{Q_p}. Counterexample on the Q_p reading: B/Q an indefinite quaternion algebra ramified at an odd p, G = B^× with V = B (Hodge type), and K_p = O_D^× = the stabilizer of O_D ⊂ D. G_{Q_p} = D^× splits over Q_{p^2} (tame), and O_D^× is the unique parahoric; the reduced building is a point, so it is special over Q_p. Over Q_p^ur it becomes Iwahori, not special. π_1(G^der) = 1. Every point of the special fibre is supersingular (basic), and the Čerednik–Drinfeld special fibre has ordinary double points. So no μ-ordinary locus is dense for any choice of embedding; indeed [b_μ] does not even exist here (E8). On the KP18 reading of 'special', the π_1 hypothesis is still missing: SU(1,5)/μ_3 acting through Λ^3 is Hodge type with π_1 = Z/3 and p = 3 > 2. KP18 Cor. 4.6.26 drops that hypothesis, but only for its abelian-type construction, which is not shown there to agree with the normalization of the closure used by KMS. The cited result does not cover the corollary's hypotheses, and on the natural reading the corollary is false.

(h_0′, h_0) factors through G″, because c∘h_0 = c′∘h_0′. G″ surjects onto G and G′ with central kernels, and G″^der ≅ G′^der. The rest of the proof is unchanged.
sourceIssues.reason: Checked on the page image. G_{V″} = GSp(V″, ψ″) (§1.3.1, p.15). G contains the scalars G_m, via the weight of X, and they map trivially to G^ad, so (1, a) ∈ G′ ×_{G^ad} G for a ∈ G_m, and {1}×G_m lies in the identity component G″. But (1, a) acts on V ⊕ V′ by (a, 1) and scales ψ″ by a² on V and by 1 on V′. It is not a symplectic similitude unless a = ±1. So G″ ⊄ G_{V″}, and 'the embedding ι″ : (G″,X″) → (G_{V″}, H_{V″})', to which 'our previous constructions' are then applied, does not exist as printed. In Noot's Mumford–Tate setting the corresponding group, the Mumford–Tate group of A × A′, automatically satisfies c = c′; the slip comes from reformulating with Shimura data. It is the same kind of slip as in the proof of Lemma 2.2.8 (E5), and the repair is routine.

With this, an element of G(Q̄_ℓ) conjugating i_ℓ to j lies in P_ℓ^T(Q̄_ℓ), and the rest of the proof goes through. The lift constructed in the proof of Proposition 2.3.11 has this property (the claim γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0′} proved there). A G(Q̄_ℓ)-element conjugating i_ℓ to j carries γ_{m,ℓ,s0} = i_ℓ(γ_{m,s0}) to j(γ_{m,s0}), which equals γ_{m,ℓ,s0'} = j(γ_{m,s0'}) only if γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0'} in T(Q). So the step quoted from the proof is incomplete, and the condition is also necessary. If f ∈ P^T(R), R ≠ 0, then f∘γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0'}∘f (f is an isogeny over F̄_p) and f∘γ_{m,s0} = j(γ_{m,s0})∘f (T-equivariance), so γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0'}. Take (j,x,s0') from Proposition 2.3.11 and let c be complex conjugation on T. By Skolem–Noether, j∘c is GL_2(Q)-conjugate to j, so (j∘c, x, s0') is again a Q̄-isogeny CM lift in the sense of §2.3.7: same image torus, same CM point, still Q̄_ℓ-conjugate to every i_ℓ, still Q̄-isogenous. review.reason: Checked on the p.34 image. The lemma asserts that P^T is a T-torsor, and the proof argues that it is non-empty, so non-emptiness is part of the claim. By 2.3.2–2.3.3, P_ℓ(s0,s0′) ⊂ Isog_ℓ consists of tensor-preserving isomorphisms that also carry γ_{m,ℓ,s0} to γ_{m,ℓ,s0′} (m sufficiently divisible). T acts on A_{s0} through T ⊂ I_{s0}. For m divisible, γ_{m,s0} is central in I_{s0}, so it lies in T(Q). T acts on A_{s0′} through j (2.3.9). Let γ′ ∈ T(Q) be the element that acts on A_{s0′} as γ_{m,s0′}. An element g ∈ G(Q̄_ℓ) with int(g)∘i_ℓ = j carries i_ℓ(γ_{m,s0}) to j(γ_{m,s0}), and that equals γ_{m,ℓ,s0′} = j(γ′) only if γ_{m,s0} = γ′. So the quoted step skips a condition. The condition is also necessary. If f ∈ P^T(R) with R ≠ 0, then f∘γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0′}∘f because f is in Isog, and f∘γ_{m,s0} = j(γ_{m,s0})∘f by T-equivariance, so γ′ = γ_{m,s0}. Counterexample: take G = GL_2 = GSp_2 (the modular curve with K_p = GL_2(Z_p); PEL type C, so Conjecture 2.3.4 holds by Lemma 2.3.5). Let s0 be an ordinary elliptic curve with End^0 = K imaginary quadratic, and T = I_{s0} = Res_{K/Q}G_m. Let (j,x,s0′) be any Q̄-isogeny CM lift (Prop. 2.3.11 gives one), and let c be the non-trivial automorphism of T. By Skolem–Noether, j∘c = int(g)∘j with g ∈ GL_2(Q). So j∘c is still Q̄_ℓ-conjugate to every i_ℓ and has the same image torus. h_x still factors through that torus, the image of Sh_{K_{T,p}}(h_x) in Sh(G,X) does not change, and P(s0,s0′) does not change either. Hence (j∘c,x,s0′) is again a Q̄-isogeny CM lift in the sense of 2.3.7, and its γ′ is c(γ′_j). If both lifts had P^T ≠ ∅, then γ_{m,s0} = γ′_j = c(γ′_j) = c(γ_{m,s0}), so π^m ∈ Q for the Frobenius π of s0. That is impossible for ordinary s0, because (π) and (π̄) are powers of the two distinct primes above p. So one of the two lifts has P^T = ∅. Starting from the lift of Prop. 2.3.11, which has γ′ = γ_{m,s0}, it is the twisted one. The defence that the paper applies the lemma only to the lift built in Prop. 2.3.11 saves Corollaries 2.3.14 and 2.3.15, but not the lemma as stated. Also, the proof of 2.3.14 only says 'a Q̄-isogeny CM lift … say (j,x,s0′)'.

review.reason: Checked on a zoomed p.35 image: 'admitting a lift to Sh_{K_{T,p}}(h_x)'. By 2.3.7, (j′,x′,s0″) is a CM lift only if s0″ lifts to the torus Shimura variety of h_{x′}, which factors through j′(T_R). This is also what [Kis17, 4.2.6] gives, which I checked. The twisted map i_ω identifies Sh(G′,X′) with Sh(G′_ω, X′_ω), where X′_ω = {ω h′ ω^{-1}}, and on it the abelian variety is the twist A_P. So P(s0,s0″) is trivial for points on the twisted locus Sh(h_{x′}). A point lifting to the old Sh(h_x) is a reduction of the old CM locus, where P(s0,s0″) is the I_{s0}-torsor induced from P^T. That torsor is not trivial in general, which is why the twist was made. Meaning clear from the construction.

Both triviality arguments given (Zariski density of Q-points of the open invertible locus; 'a product of inner forms of GL_n', up to Weil restriction) work for any semisimple algebra, so the conclusion stands.

review.reason: Checked on the p.36 image. When only endomorphisms are respected, the analogue of P(s0,s0′) is a torsor under Aut_B(A_{s0}) = (End_B(A_{s0}) ⊗ Q)^×. End_B(A_{s0}) ⊗ Q is a semisimple Q-algebra: a product of matrix algebras over division algebras, not in general a product of skew fields. For example, on the genus-2 Siegel variety (B = Q), a supersingular A_{s0} ≅ E×E has End^0 = M_2(D_{p,∞}). Both arguments for triviality still work: a torsor under the units of a semisimple algebra is a non-empty open subscheme of an affine space over Q, so it has a Q-point; and the group is a product of Weil restrictions of inner forms of GL_n. The authors' own phrase 'inner forms of GL_n' fits the correct description, so the slip is only in the wording. The conclusion stands.

sourceIssues.correction: The reduction step must also make A ×_U U_i extend to a semi-abelian scheme over S_i. One way: take a proper S̄ ⊃ U over which A extends semi-abelianly, and apply [dJ96, 6.5] to S̄ with Z = S̄∖U (and likewise to build U_1). Then the S_i map to S̄ and the extension pulls back. In the application such an S̄ is a toroidal compactification [MP19]. In general one can first pass to the finite étale cover of U trivializing A[N] (N ≥ 3, p ∤ N; this is harmless for proper descent) and use a toroidal compactification of the moduli space [FC] (A polarizable) to get such an S̄. Alternatively, Raynaud's criterion gives semi-abelian reduction at the generic points of S_i∖U_i, and one then extends across the normal-crossings boundary of the regular S_i.
sourceIssues.reason: Proposition A.6 is stated in the setting of A.2–A.3, which requires the abelian scheme over U to extend to a semi-abelian scheme over S. That hypothesis produces E^log via [MP19, 1.3.5] and underlies Lemma A.4. [dJ96, Thm 6.5] only provides a semi-stable compactification S_i of U_i, and the pulled-back abelian scheme need not extend semi-abelianly across the new boundary S_i∖U_i. Example: the Legendre family over U = Spec W[λ, 1/λ(1−λ)] with S = U, D = ∅. The choice U_0 = U, S_0 = P^1_W (after a finite extension) satisfies everything the proof asks of de Jong's theorem, but the curve has non-unipotent (−1 times unipotent) monodromy, hence additive reduction, at λ = ∞. So the reduction step as written can fail. The statement of Corollary A.7 is very likely true with the repair above. By p.19, Proposition 1.3.12 (and so this appendix) is used only in (1.3.14) and (1.3.16).

review.reason: Checked on the p.39 image, and against A.2–A.3 (pp.37–38). Proposition A.6 is stated in the setting of A.2–A.3. That setting requires the abelian scheme over U to extend to a semi-abelian scheme over S, which produces E^log through [MP19, 1.3.5] and hence E^vlog and Lemma A.4. Corollary A.7 assumes this only for the original S ('as above'). The proof replaces (U,S) by (U_i,S_i), where the S_i are the compactifications given by [dJ96, 6.5]. Nothing ensures that A ×_U U_i extends semi-abelianly over the new boundary S_i∖U_i. Since S_i is proper and S need not be, S_i does not in general map to S, so the extension cannot simply be pulled back. Example (p > 2): the Legendre family y² = x(x−1)(x−λ) over U = S = Spec W[λ, 1/λ(1−λ)], with D = ∅. The choice U_1 = U_0 = U and S_0 = S_1 = P^1_W meets every requirement the proof places on de Jong's output: P^1_W is smooth over W, and the disjoint sections 0, 1, ∞ together with the special fibre form a strict normal crossings divisor. But at λ = ∞ the curve is the quadratic twist by the uniformizer of an I_2 curve. It has type I_2^* (additive) reduction, with local monodromy −(unipotent), so it does not extend semi-abelianly over the generic point of the ∞-section, and Proposition A.6 cannot be applied. In the application to Proposition 1.3.12 the base is the non-proper integral model, so new boundary really occurs. The statement of A.7 is very likely true with a repair, so this is a gap in the proof. Per p.19, Proposition 1.3.12 is only used in §1.3 (Cor. 1.3.13, (1.3.14), (1.3.16)).
